THOUGHT: The patient is a 23-year-old male recently diagnosed with schizophrenia and initiated on risperidone two months ago. He reports marked improvement in psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, paranoia), confirming treatment efficacy. However, he now presents with new-onset subjective restlessness, inability to remain still, fidgeting, leg crossing/uncrossing, and pacing — all occurring in the absence of objective involuntary movements (e.g., tremor, chorea, dystonia) on exam, and with normal neurological examination otherwise (normal tone, strength, coordination, gait *except* for purposeful ambulation due to restlessness). Vital signs and laboratory studies (CBC, LFTs, electrolytes, thyroid function) are unremarkable, ruling out metabolic, infectious, or endocrine causes of agitation or movement disturbance. The temporal association — onset ~2 months after starting risperidone — strongly implicates medication-induced akathisia. Risperidone is a high-potency dopamine D2 receptor antagonist with well-documented risk for akathisia, especially during early treatment or dose escalation. Akathisia is characterized by a subjective sense of inner restlessness and an objective need to move, often manifesting as pacing, rocking, or repetitive leg movements — precisely matching this patient’s presentation. While other drug-induced movement disorders (e.g., parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia) are possible, they typically present later (tardive dyskinesia usually >3–6 months), involve observable abnormal movements (not just restlessness), and are not consistent with the exam findings here (no bradykinesia, rigidity, or orofacial/buccolingual movements). Anxiety or agitation due to residual psychosis is unlikely given his clear report and observed improvement in psychotic symptoms and mental status exam.

DIAGNOSIS: Antipsychotic-induced akathisia
